# Drivers

**Lab 4.** Every driver is a `Driver` vtable, registered at boot as a comptime list (`drivers/registry.zig`):

```zig
pub const Driver = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    init: fn () Error!void,
    probe: fn () bool,
    shutdown: fn () void,
};
```

## Built-in drivers

```
drivers/
├── bus/
│   └── pci.zig          // PCI enumeration
├── char/
│   ├── uart.zig         // COM1 serial port (debug)
│   └── keyboard.zig     // PS/2 keyboard (IRQ1)
├── video/
│   ├── vga.zig          // VGA text mode 0xB8000
│   └── framebuffer.zig  // Limine framebuffer
└── timer/
    └── pit.zig          // 8254 PIT → scheduler tick
```

Interrupt handlers are minimal by rule: acknowledge, queue, return — no allocation in the ISR. The block layer (Phase 6) adds a VirtIO-block reader plus PCI common-config access.

## The UART experiment

UART is the first *research* driver (see `docs/UART.md`), deliberately kept small:

> Send the byte 0x41 through a UART.

Not a serial subsystem — a laboratory for the whole pipeline: hardware documentation → AI → Driver Plan → capabilities → generated hardware logic → validation → isolation → execution. Later stages add init, receive, interrupts, concurrency, and error handling only once the measurement questions of each stage are answered.

## Lab 4 — driver markers

```bash
zig build boot-test
# Expected serial lines (among others):
# PCI scan OK, VirtIO block read OK
# Keyboard init/test OK, VFS test OK, tmpfs test OK
```

Then read `kernel/drivers/char/uart.zig`: it is the reference example of over-documented hardware code — every register meaning, ordering assumption, and quirk is commented where it happens.
